items.question: Why do you see learning a source of interactive environments as important for training generalist reinforcement learning agents?
items.object: Learning environments for training generalist reinforcement learning agents
items.answer: Typically, as reinforcement learning researchers, we often get a little bit annoyed with how we have to bring in more and more environments. Typically, if you want to train an agent, you're like, “Okay, well, maybe I can bring this in or bring this in,” but this doesn't really scale. Nowadays, we're interested in generalist agents, and if we want generalist reinforcement learning agents, where do the environments come from? One of the motivations behind that work was: How can we basically learn an unlimited source of environments for training agents? It gives you the sort of interactivity that you would have in an RL environment without actually having to place the agent within the environment itself.
quotes: Typically, as reinforcement learning researchers, we often get a little bit annoyed with how we have to bring in more and more environments. Typically, if you want to train an agent, you're like, “Okay, well, maybe I can bring this in or bring this in,” but this doesn't really scale.
Nowadays, we're interested in generalist agents, and if we want generalist reinforcement learning agents, where do the environments come from?

One of the motivations behind that work was: How can we basically learn an unlimited source of environments for training agents? It gives you the sort of interactivity that you would have in an RL environment without actually having to place the agent within the environment itself.

rubrics.text: The response states that manually adding training environments does not scale to training generalist reinforcement learning agents.
The response states that learned environments can provide reinforcement-learning-style interactivity without placing the agent in the underlying environment itself.

items.question: How do you see the value of learning from videos to train reinforcement learning agents?
items.object: Learning from videos to train reinforcement learning agents
items.answer: Often, when you're doing RL or imitation learning, you typically need annotations of states and actions that tell you what to do, but often it's kind of difficult to come up with those demonstrations. It requires a lot of effort on the demonstrator. My research has been about how we can leverage videos to train agents: how we can learn action policies and rewards for training reinforcement learning agents. That is one of the areas where Genie is unique, because you're learning all of these actions in a totally unsupervised way.
quotes: Often, when you're doing RL or imitation learning, you typically need annotations of states and actions that tell you what to do, but often it's kind of difficult to come up with those demonstrations. It requires a lot of effort on the demonstrator.

items.question: How did you think about the choice of training data sources for Genie?
items.object: Genie's training data sources
items.answer: In the paper, we basically use two different kinds of sources of data. The main one would be videos of 2D platformer games. In reinforcement learning, we love training over games, so we kind of looked into that sort of environment: a very diverse dataset with lots of different actions and different agents moving around. The other one is a robotics dataset coming from, I think it was RT-1, Q-Top. We extracted the observations without actions from that environment and trained as well, just to show that we can also use this approach on real-world environments.

items.question: What excites you most about Genie's ability to learn an interactive world model from videos?
items.object: Genie's unsupervised learning of interactive world models
items.answer: The thing that really excites me the most is that you can learn this sort of world model without using any actions. You can learn it completely unsupervised from videos, which is quite general. You don't need many inductive biases here; you just give it a bunch of videos and it learns a world model that you can interact with. What we found was, in particular when we were training over the 2D platformer games, that we can take text-generated images, sketches, or real-world photos and sort of just step into those environments as if they were a real game. We could basically play it like it was a real world model, even though we didn't use actions at all here or learn ground-truth actions.

items.question: How do you understand what makes Genie a world model?
items.object: World models and Genie's generalization across 2D platformer games
items.answer: When I think of the world model, I really think of something that you can step into and interact with. If you remember Schmidhuber and David Ha's paper from a while ago, I think they did Doom. They had this world model paper, and then you've learned a simulator of Doom. items.question: How do you frame the learning problem for Genie's latent action model when working with gameplay videos?
items.object: Genie's latent action model
items.answer: I'm sure that sort of information—labels showing which controls were pressed—could have been in there, but it wasn't something that we were explicitly trying to extract. Mainly, what we were trying to figure out is: Can you learn a representation of what's going to change between the scenes so that you can predict the next frame? This is basically what our inductive assumptions are.

items.question: How do you think about the assumptions behind Genie's action space?
items.object: Genie's restricted, shared action space
items.answer: I think one thing I would say is we try to restrict the action space so that we can actually interact with it. Basically, we're representing our actions using a discrete codebook, using vector quantization. One, we assumed that we had a small set of actions, which is definitely not the case, but it just made it easier for us to interact with the models. The other thing that we assumed was that there was a common action space across the different environments that we were training on. This was going to allow us to learn this sort of general representation, because we're learning over all of these environments. We wanted to learn what was common: there must be different agents that are going to move to the left or move to the right or jump, and we wanted to learn the representation that captured that.

items.question: Why do you see attention over all the image patches in a video as computationally impractical for Genie?
items.object: Attention over all image patches in a video Transformer
items.answer: Essentially, what we need to do is we need a representation of our images. We represent them through patches, again using vector quantization. Each image is represented by a patch, essentially, so you have a sequence of images, which is your video. If we were going to try to plug in each of those patches into our Transformer and basically have attention over all of those different patches, we would end up with something very computationally intractable.
quotes: Essentially, what we need to do is we need a representation of our images. We represent them through patches, again using vector quantization. Each image is represented by a patch, essentially, so you have a sequence of images, which is your video. If we were going to try to plug in each of those patches into our Transformer and basically have attention over all of those different patches, we would end up with something very computationally intractable.

items.question: How do you think Genie's architecture could evolve to make video generation more efficient?
items.object: Alternatives to Genie's Transformer architecture for more efficient video generation
items.answer: The context window of Genie, I think, was maybe 16 frames. If we wanted to roll out, or once we start looking into longer generations, I think it might make sense to look into these more efficient approaches, like they do in state space models. One thing that I find interesting is that we have to put our images into these patches just so that we can have tokens for the Transformer to predict. I mean, it works. I think it works well, but I do think that there are probably other ways that we can represent images. You also have diffusion, which you can do over latent space rather than having to predict over patches necessarily. In general, when we built this model, we were looking at, “Okay, this is a thing that's probably going to work,” and we put those things together. But now I think there are probably different ways that we can improve upon each of the different components that we had in the model in terms of making it more efficient.

items.question: How do you think about the role of compression in Genie's latent action model?
items.object: Compression in Genie's latent action model
items.answer: Let's start with just imagine we have two frames. Say you have two frames; what you want to do is learn a representation that you're going to press such that, if you take that representation in your previous frame, you can predict the next frame. The latent action model gets to see both the past and the future, but we compress it in such a way that you can't actually extract the information about the state itself. You really just have to try to extract the change that occurs between states so you can use it for predicting the future. The way we compress it is we place it through a bottleneck, and then we put it through this PQ module. We have ten codes, and we're trying to learn to make our representations be close to those codes that we're also learning at the same time.

items.question: How do you explain Genie's ability to learn a consistent latent action mapping across different environments?
items.object: Genie's consistent latent action mapping across environments
items.answer: Surprisingly, it does learn this sort of consistent mapping across different inputs. Latent action zero might always mean move to the left; move right might always be latent action four. We didn't do anything to actually ground the action space in this, but I think it's just through the fact that the model needs to learn this representation in order to predict the future, and it's easier for it to learn the same thing across different environments.

items.question: How do you think about measuring the performance of interactive models?
items.object: Evaluation of interactive models
items.answer: With interactive models, it's really hard to measure things like controllability, but you can measure things like video quality. We're using metrics like FVD, for example, to measure how good the videos are.

items.question: What did you find when comparing the SeViT architecture with a spatiotemporal Transformer?
items.object: SeViT architecture compared with a spatiotemporal Transformer
items.answer: We looked at a couple of different representations compared to using a spatiotemporal Transformer. One of them was the SeViT architecture, which was used in FVD. In general, because they don't do this spatiotemporal trick where you only attend to one token over time, you have to attend over multiple frames, so it was quite compute intensive. That was the main architecture I think we compared to.
quotes: We looked at a couple of different representations compared to using a spatiotemporal Transformer. One of them was the SeViT architecture, which was used in FVD. That was the main architecture I think we compared to.

rubrics.text: The response attributes SeViT’s high computational cost to attending across multiple frames rather than restricting temporal attention to a single token as the compared spatiotemporal Transformer does.

items.question: Why did you choose a spatiotemporal video tokenization scheme for Genie?
items.object: Genie's video tokenization scheme
items.answer: One thing is that it enables us to predict tokens with the dynamics model. Because we were doing video generation, if we were predicting pixels themselves, then we would end up getting blurry generations. We probably wouldn't want to use a convolutional neural network in this case. Because we put it into patches, we can predict a discrete patch—we use vector quantization for that—so we can predict a discrete patch that we can then plug into the decoder to reconstruct the image, rather than having to predict the image itself. That led us to get sharp predictions from the model. The other thing is that the spatiotemporal component was important because, if we were tokenizing only in space, it might not represent the sorts of changes that you need to represent when you're predicting the next frame. If we were only using this for image generation, we obviously wouldn't need the temporal part, because you don't have it. But because we're generating videos, it's useful to have an architecture that can capture changes across time. Those were the main reasons we looked into using this sort of tokenization scheme. The spatiotemporal model is what we ended up using in every component. The video tokenizer wasn't used in the latent action model; we just used it in the decoder. But we used the spatiotemporal architecture in the video tokenizer, the latent action model, and the dynamics model.

items.question: How do you think about the possibility of training Genie as a single end-to-end model?
items.object: Training Genie as a single end-to-end model
items.answer: It's something that we wanted to get working throughout the project. The thing that was most frustrating—or, I mean, annoying—was that our latent action model has its own decoder. It takes state, next state, goes into the action model, predicts the next state. That decoder is different from our dynamics model. The dynamics model is taking the state and latent action and predicting the next state. We could never get that model to train our latent actions. It was very difficult. One thing is that we're training it in a different way. That model first of all takes in tokens. We found that training directly on pixels for the latent action model performed better than training on tokens for it. That model outputs tokens, and we found that predicting pixels helped the latent action model perform better. It might just be a difference in the kinds of losses that we had: the dynamics model uses a cross-entropy loss, whereas the latent action model uses mean squared error loss. It could maybe be possible to train a tokenizer at the same time as a latent action model, but I'm sure there's a way to make it end to end. We found the way that worked, and I think the next step maybe would be to make it more elegant. I wish that it was end to end, but it's not.

items.question: How do you use tokens to predict video patches in Genie's dynamics model?
items.object: Token prediction in Genie's dynamics model
items.answer: Our dynamics model outputs patches, but it's predicting the tokens. The way our video tokenizer works is you get patches, we place that through a VQ module, which gives it a discrete code for each of those kinds of patches. Then what we can do for our dynamics model is predict patches, but they're represented through tokens, so you can use a cross-entropy loss over those different patches. One thing is that we're doing masked token prediction rather than predicting all the tokens at the same time, at least during training. During inference time, of course, you have to predict all of the tokens.

items.question: How do you distinguish spatial attention from temporal attention when representing images as sequences of patches?
items.object: Spatial and temporal attention over image patches
items.answer: I'm going to go through this image, and each of these parts are going to correspond to a patch. I can then represent that as a sequence, so that that particular image is represented by a sequence of patches. We have the spatial part and the temporal part. The spatial Transformer is attending across patches in a single image, and the temporal part attends to a particular patch across time. It's only attending to that single patch, that same patch, over time.

We have the spatial part and the temporal part. The spatial part gets to see—the spatial Transformer is attending across patches in a single image, and the temporal part attends to a particular patch across time. It's only attending to that single patch, that same patch, over time.

items.question: How do you think about MaskGIT as a way of predicting tokens during inference?
items.object: MaskGIT for token prediction during inference
items.answer: We're using a technique known as MaskGIT during inference time. Rather than predicting a single token one by one, you predict them in parallel. You unmask some tokens, keep the ones that you're most confident about, and then condition your model again on those, and then you predict the next tokens, essentially. So this is MaskGIT, as compared to—I mean, I guess what most people are using these days is diffusion. You're predicting tokens based on the masked sequence of patches.
quotes: We're using a technique known as MaskGIT during inference time. Rather than predicting a single token one by one, you predict them in parallel. You unmask some tokens, keep the ones that you're most confident about, and then condition your model again on those, and then you predict the next tokens, essentially. So this is MaskGIT, as compared to—I mean, I guess what most people are using these days is diffusion. You're predicting tokens based on the masked sequence of patches.

rubrics.text: The response states that MaskGIT predicts tokens in parallel rather than one token at a time.
The response states that MaskGIT retains the token predictions in which the model is most confident.

items.question: How do you assess Genie's consistency during extended play?
items.object: Genie's action consistency and environmental behavior during extended play
items.answer: The actions are able to remain consistent. It does tend to maybe overfit as you press the same action. For example, if you've been taking action right, over time I would say the actions might end up all going right. We found that there's an action that would say, “Okay, stop doing that,” and switch, which is kind of weird, but there's an action you can take that would let you start moving left again. I guess it's like a stay-still-and-then-change-direction style thing. If you're moving right for a long time, you generally just see a pattern of the background moving over and over again. You keep seeing the same things. I don't think I've ever seen anything in our out-of-distribution environments; I don't think I've ever seen anything interesting pop up out of nowhere, essentially.

items.question: How do you explain why a latent action in Genie might stop producing the expected change in direction after prolonged movement?
items.object: Changes in the effect of latent actions during interaction with Genie
items.answer: The actions, given different prompt frames, taking latent action zero typically would move you to the left or right or whatever across different initial frames. Over time, if you've played the environment and you've been taking the same action, certain things might have to do with velocity. I think it's learned a model of how the world is going to work. If you're going up and continuing to go up, it's very difficult to start going down or take the action that's going to go down, because the model has predicted, and it's a model of maybe the physics of the world, that you can't suddenly start going down. It might be ignoring the latent action predictions because it knows that it's very rare that you would suddenly start moving left. It might just be two things: one, it could be ignoring because of the physics of the world; two, it could be ignoring because of the policies that it's trained with. Maybe people typically don't suddenly go left when they've been going right for a while.

items.question: How did you come to understand Genie's ability to turn generated images, sketches, and real photos into controllable environments?
items.object: Genie's ability to generate controllable environments from different image sources
items.answer: It just kind of worked. It was actually really crazy. We used to have this thing called the Genie Bottle Challenge. We would all get together and play our environments and see if we could reach a genie lamp that was generated from a text-generated image. The model in the beginning was really bad. Eventually we were able to reach the genie lamp. Once we solved that challenge, we started thinking about what other sources of data would work. At some point, we asked Jeff Clune's children, Caspian and Cica, to make these sketches that we have in the paper. We played those environments, and I think Richie also drew a really cool sketch, and you can climb up the ladder. At some point someone was like, “What if we plugged in real photos?” I was like, “Why would that work? We trained over platformer games.” But then we were able to control Jack's dog, Doris. For whatever reason, she looks like a character in the middle of a screen, I guess, so we were able to move her around. We didn't do anything different; we just plugged them in.

items.question: How do you understand the difficulty of getting Genie to control the part of an environment you intend?
items.object: Selecting what to control in a Genie-generated environment
items.answer: One other thing I forgot to mention is it can sometimes be difficult to figure out what you want to control in the environment. Maybe you want to control the clouds in the sky rather than the dog. If you take an action that controls the right thing, then all of the actions start controlling the right thing. Initially, they might be controlling different parts of the scene, but as soon as you take an action that's controlling the thing you want to control, all of a sudden they start controlling it too.

items.question: How do you see video input helping Genie control a particular part of a scene?
items.object: Using video input to control a particular part of a scene in Genie
items.answer: Actually, if you plug in a video, it's much easier to control a given part of it. If you've given it some video, you can figure out what to control. Essentially, what you have to do is infer the actions. You feed in a frame, infer all the actions, roll that out into the model, and then you can predict the next frame given that context. I don't think we put any results in the paper about this, but it was something that we saw.

items.question: How do you see the potential for adding interactive control to generated video scenes?
items.object: Adding interactive control to generated video scenes
items.answer: I think it's a good point: we can build upon these things and get the kind of controllability that you wouldn't necessarily get initially from the model, but now have nice generated scenes that you can then take over. If you've trained on that sort of data, it wouldn't work on the 2D platformer one. We controlled the dog, but I doubt it would work on 3D.

items.question: How do you see Genie's potential beyond creating interactive environments for reinforcement learning researchers?
items.object: Genie's broader uses beyond reinforcement learning
items.answer: When we started, we were definitely interested in using it for reinforcement learning. Over time, we realized it was fun to actually interact with it. This is why we started looking into sketches and people's drawings. When we put out the paper, people reached out to us from places I wouldn't have expected: teachers interested in using this sort of model for their students; people who had video-only data and were trying to learn simulations of that data that they can use, maybe also as teaching tools; and people in the industry. It's just something fun for creatives to work with. There are many different kinds of areas that it could be used for.

items.question: How do you assess Genie's potential for making playable games?
items.object: Genie’s potential for making playable games
items.answer: One of the gaps is inference speed. You can't really interact with these in real time. The videos that we generated were not in real time; they were just a video of us interacting with them, but it was probably one frame per second. That's one thing: trying to speed up inference. But also, whether this is something you would want to do is an important question. Making sure that you're having conversations with people who would also be impacted by this technology early on would be important. I don't think Genie is something I would play as a game at this point in time, but it is fun. It's a very different kind of game, so it's not something that's going to take over your favorite video game. I think it could be a new form of interactive media that people can interact with.

items.question: Why did you choose human interaction to demonstrate the environments generated by Genie?
items.object: Human interaction versus random actions for demonstrating Genie-generated environments
items.answer: That was how we generated most of them, unfortunately. We have this video on the website that shows a zooming out on all the environments you can generate with Genie. That was all real gameplay of people stepping into the environment and interacting, because random behavior doesn't look interesting. If you plug in a random sequence of actions, you would just see things jittering around; it doesn't look that interesting. We wanted to have things that look like real gameplay. The alternative would be to maybe generate a game tree over time, but that would take a really long time to do. So, yeah, we did it ourselves.

items.question: How do you see your shift from reinforcement learning to video generation?
items.object: The shift from reinforcement learning to video generation
items.answer: It's been interesting to see my shift from doing reinforcement learning to working on video generation, although I've always done reinforcement learning from videos, actually, so it's not that crazy of a shift. It's really cool to start looking into the different kinds of methods that people have been using. This approach was MaskGIT. Now I'm getting more interested in diffusion, which is a completely different area from what I'm used to, but it's been fun to learn about that space.
